Hi all,

I'm curious how everyone's agents are doing on the 25 public demo games, and I think it would help all of us to have a rough community baseline in one place. Local public-game results aren't a perfect leaderboard proxy, but they're still the fastest signal most of us have while iterating.

If you're willing to share, here's a format that would make comparison easy:

Overall: average score across the 25 games (and how many games you score > 0 on) Per game: which games you clear, and roughly what score — even a rough "solved / partially solved / zero" breakdown is useful Setup: base model, harness style (coding agent in a REPL, orchestrator + subagents, RL, hand-written search, etc.) Budget: actions per game and wall-clock/compute per game Gap: how your local public-game numbers compare to your leaderboard submission

A few things I'd love to hear discussion on:

Which of the 25 games are the "wall" games that almost nothing clears? Are they hard for a shared reason (long horizons? hidden state? unclear win conditions?), or hard in different ways? Are people's scores mostly limited by not beating levels, or by beating them with far more actions than humans? Those point to very different fixes. How much variance do you see across repeated runs on the same game with the same agent? I want to know how much of a score delta is signal vs. noise. Has anyone found a small subset of the public games that predicts leaderboard performance well? Running all 25 every iteration is expensive.

I'll share my own numbers in the comments to get things started. Thanks!

And because I am out of you know whats, most of what I have done is just take the stock duck client for nvp4 and increase the sequence concurrency to 16. Anything else I have done, and it's a lot, amounted to jack

That will get you to the brink of the top 10%, but all of my harness engineering beyond that has been utterly useless. And now I learned that the winner isn't going to be who scored highest on the 55 truly hidden games, but your best lottery ticket based on how it did on the other 55.

To that end, I tasked Astra, the supposed AGI according who absolutely know better, to build a new harness. After 2 days, it scores about as well as duck. And that is where I am starting to conclude that any further progress requires SFT/RL on an existing model or maybe training a jev-like alternative. Starting to not care honestly. The score here is more resource constrained than anything else and that's really not that much fun.

the leaderboard problems are completely unseen so doing well on the public problems does not guarantee a high score on the hidden games.

It's worse than that. They are both unseen and you have to choose two of your seen hidden scores to guess which ones scored the best on the unseen hidden scores that determine the winner. How is that a good idea?

you have to choose two of your seen hidden scores to guess which ones scored the best on the unseen hidden scores that determine the winner. How is that a good idea?

It is THE GOOD IDEA of Kaggle.

It is set this way to test how well your pipeline generalizes to new, unseen data.

The purpose of machine learning is to build models that perform well on new data.

If you don't have a hidden test set, then you might build a model or pipeline that works great on the public test data but that would perform badly on new data. Your model would look good when it is useless. This bad outcome is called overfitting in ML. The hidden test set purpose is to check for overfitting.

The real issue is that most benchmark out there have only public test data. People report awesome numbers on these for their LLMs, only for people to be disappointed when they apply these LLMs to new data.

In LLM folklore this is known as benchmaxing, but it is the same as overfitting.

It is a good idea tho, isnt it basically the core of this competition? To see how well we can make a model can generalize on unseen tasks, given limited resources? And anyways, competitions like these are how we can actually evaluate how good a model does, ppl have been benchmaxxing a lot.

Recently: Public 7.6% (solving 35 levels total) -> 3.35% Private LB, Public 10.2% (solving 44 levels total) -> 3.05% Private LB, Public 7.7% (solving 37 levels total) -> 4.42% Private LB

It almost feels like doing better on the public set (even without any game-specific stuff) correlates to weaker private scores.

Also all those above scores were different harness variations. It feels almost impossible to experiment because you need to submit at least like 5 times to get a good feel for how a notebook version scores (to account for the variation), but with only 1 submission a day the progress is so slow.
